lead: Page‑replacement algorithms decide which page to evict when a new page is needed and all frames are occupied. They keep the system running without running out of memory and affect overall speed. FIFO, LRU and the theoretical optimal algorithm are the three most taught methods. They are used in any OS that supports virtual memory, from mobile phones handling app switching to servers running many processes.
prereq: You need: Virtual memory, demand paging, page faults, copy‑on‑write.

blocks.text: FIFO keeps pages in the order they entered memory. When a replacement is needed, the page that has been in memory the longest is removed, regardless of how often it was used.

items: Maintain a queue of pages currently in frames.
On a page fault, if a free frame exists, insert the page at the tail of the queue.
If all frames are full, remove the page at the head of the queue and insert the new page at the tail.
Simple to implement with a circular buffer.
Can suffer from Belady’s anomaly – more frames may cause more faults.

blocks.text: F_faults = number of page references that are not in the current frame set
blocks.where: F_faults counts each miss; the algorithm does not use any future information.

blocks.text: LRU replaces the page that has not been used for the longest time. It approximates the optimal algorithm by using past information.

items: Maintain a stack with most‑recently used page on top.
On a hit, move the page to the top of the stack.
On a fault, if a free frame exists, push the new page on top.
If no free frame, pop the bottom page (least recent) and push the new page.

blocks.text: Optimal (Belady) replaces the page whose next use is farthest in the future. It gives the minimum possible faults for a given reference string but cannot be implemented online.

items: LRU can be implemented with hardware support such as reference bits, or approximated by algorithms like the Clock (second‑chance) method.
Optimal is used only for analysis and to benchmark other algorithms.

spec.title: Reference string simulation

examples.question: Reference string: 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 with 3 frames. Compute the number of page faults for FIFO, LRU and Optimal replacement.
steps: Process each reference in order, applying the chosen algorithm.
Count a fault whenever the referenced page is not already in a frame.
For FIFO, evict the page that entered earliest when needed.
For LRU, evict the page whose last use is oldest.
For Optimal, look ahead and evict the page whose next use is farthest (or never used).
examples.answer: FIFO: 9 faults, LRU: 10 faults, Optimal: 7 faults.

traps: Assuming LRU always gives fewer faults than FIFO; the example shows both can have the same count.
Counting a hit as a fault when the page is already in a frame.
For Optimal, forgetting to look ahead far enough and evicting a page that will be used soon.
Confusing the order of replacement in FIFO (oldest entry) with LRU (oldest use).

quiz.q: What does FIFO stand for in page replacement?
Why can FIFO cause more page faults when the number of frames increases?
quiz.a: Because of Belady’s anomaly – the order of arrivals may lead to evicting pages that will be needed soon, increasing faults.

quiz.q: Given the reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 with 3 frames, how many faults does LRU incur?
quiz.a: Step through the string using the LRU stack; the total faults are 9.

quiz.q: Write a short Python function that returns the number of FIFO faults for any reference string and frame count.
Explain why the optimal algorithm cannot be used in a real operating system.
quiz.a: It requires knowledge of future references, which the OS does not have; therefore it can only be used for theoretical comparison.

quiz.q: A system shows 12 page faults with FIFO and 10 with LRU for a workload. Does this guarantee that LRU is always better? Justify.
quiz.a: No. Page‑fault count depends on the specific reference pattern; some patterns give equal or even fewer FIFO faults. LRU is generally better but not universally.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern cloud servers, page‑replacement decisions are guided by machine‑learning models that predict future accesses, extending the optimal idea. Research explores adaptive algorithms that switch between FIFO, LRU, and clock variants based on workload characteristics. Mobile operating systems use trimmed versions to save power, often combining LRU with frequency counters. Emerging non‑volatile RAM changes the cost model of page faults, prompting new replacement strategies. Look for recent papers on "learning‑augmented page replacement" and on the Linux "zswap" and "zram" subsystems for practical implementations.
